title: Manakish with cheese
subtitle: Flatbread topped with melted halloumi and sesame
excerpt: Manakish are small Lebanese flatbreads baked with toppings pressed directly into the dough. The cheese version uses halloumi, which melts without splitting and gives a slightly salty, springy topping on the soft bread. Eaten hot for breakfast or a quick lunch.
sourceNotes: Anissa Helou, Lebanese Cuisine (1994). Manakish described as the most common Levantine breakfast bread, made fresh each morning by home bakers and street vendors. Claudia Roden, The Food of the Middle East (1974).

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze baked flatbreads before adding toppings. Reheat in a hot oven for five minutes and add toppings fresh.
recipe.batchNotes: Double the dough and freeze half for another time.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The dough can rest in the fridge overnight after the first rise. Bring back to room temperature before shaping.
recipe.temperatureNote: Fan 210 degrees / gas 8. Preheat for at least 20 minutes.

content.text: Manakish are Lebanese breakfast flatbreads, small and soft with toppings pressed into the surface before baking. The cheese version is topped with grated halloumi, which holds its shape under heat and gives a lightly browned, salty surface. The dough takes an hour to rise and ten minutes to bake.
Mix {{yeast-dried}} and {{caster-sugar}} into 185 ml of warm water and leave for five minutes until foamy.

Combine {{strong-bread-flour}} and {{sea-salt-fine}} in a large bowl. Add the yeast liquid and {{olive-oil}}. Stir to a rough dough, then knead on a lightly floured surface for eight minutes until smooth and elastic.
Return to the bowl, cover with a damp cloth, and leave in a warm place for one hour until doubled in size.
Preheat the oven to 230 degrees. If you have a baking stone, preheat that too. Otherwise line two baking trays.
Divide the dough into four equal pieces. On a lightly floured surface, flatten each piece into a rough disc about 20 cm across and 3 mm thick. It does not need to be perfectly round.
Lay the discs on the lined trays. Scatter {{halloumi}} over each one, pressing it lightly into the surface. Scatter {{sesame-seeds}} over the top and drizzle with {{extra-virgin-olive-oil}}.
Bake for 10 to 12 minutes until the edges are golden and the cheese is melted and lightly browned in patches. Eat immediately, while the bread is soft and the cheese is still molten.

items.symptom: The base is doughy and undercooked
items.cause: Oven not hot enough or dough too thick
items.fix: The oven must be fully preheated to 230 degrees before the bread goes in. Roll the discs to no more than 3 mm. A hot baking tray helps the base cook faster.

items.symptom: The cheese slides off during baking
items.cause: Not pressed into the dough before baking
items.fix: Press the grated halloumi firmly onto the surface after topping. The drizzle of oil also helps it adhere.

items.cause: Yeast was added to water that was too hot
items.fix: Water above 45 degrees kills yeast. It should feel warm but not hot to the touch. Restart with new yeast and water at 38 to 40 degrees.

items.cause: Dough was overworked or the bread cooled before eating
items.fix: Manakish must be eaten fresh from the oven. They toughen as they cool. Knead for the time specified, no longer.

content.text: Manakish are the Lebanese equivalent of a breakfast pastry: bought fresh from the furn (communal bakery) every morning and eaten on the way to school or work. The bakery opens at dawn and the flatbreads come out in continuous batches. The two most common versions are cheese and za'atar. The cheese is traditionally a stretched curd cheese called akkawi, mild and salty; halloumi behaves similarly when heated and is the most available substitute outside the Levant. Manakish are also made at home at weekends, particularly for family breakfast. The dough is deliberately soft and pillowy rather than crisp.
